commit_message:
ipf: release unhandled packets from the batch

Since 640d4db788ed ("ipf: Fix a use-after-free error, ...") the ipf
framework unconditionally allocates a new dp_packet to track
individual fragments.  This prevents a use-after-free.  However, an
additional issue was present - even when the packet buffer is cloned,
if the ip fragment handling code keeps it, the original buffer is
leaked during the refill loop.  Even in the original processing code,
the hardcoded dnsteal branches would always leak a packet buffer from
the refill loop.

This can be confirmed with valgrind:

==717566== 16,672 (4,480 direct, 12,192 indirect) bytes in 8 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 390 of 390
==717566==    at 0x484086F: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:380)
==717566==    by 0x537BFD: xmalloc__ (util.c:137)
==717566==    by 0x537BFD: xmalloc (util.c:172)
==717566==    by 0x46DDD4: dp_packet_new (dp-packet.c:153)
==717566==    by 0x46DDD4: dp_packet_new_with_headroom (dp-packet.c:163)
==717566==    by 0x550AA6: netdev_linux_batch_rxq_recv_sock.constprop.0 (netdev-linux.c:1262)
==717566==    by 0x5512AF: netdev_linux_rxq_recv (netdev-linux.c:1511)
==717566==    by 0x4AB7E0: netdev_rxq_recv (netdev.c:727)
==717566==    by 0x47F00D: dp_netdev_process_rxq_port (dpif-netdev.c:4699)
==717566==    by 0x47FD13: dpif_netdev_run (dpif-netdev.c:5957)
==717566==    by 0x4331D2: type_run (ofproto-dpif.c:370)
==717566==    by 0x41DFD8: ofproto_type_run (ofproto.c:1768)
==717566==    by 0x40A7FB: bridge_run__ (bridge.c:3245)
==717566==    by 0x411269: bridge_run (bridge.c:3310)
==717566==    by 0x406E6C: main (ovs-vswitchd.c:127)

The fix is to delete the original packet when it isn't able to be
reinserted into the packet batch.  Subsequent valgrind runs show that
the packets are not leaked from the batch any longer.

Fixes: 640d4db788ed ("ipf: Fix a use-after-free error, and remove the 'do_not_steal' flag.")
Fixes: 4ea96698f667 ("Userspace datapath: Add fragmentation handling.")
Reported-by: Wan Junjie <wanjunjie@bytedance.com>
Reported-at: https://github.com/openvswitch/ovs-issues/issues/226
Signed-off-by: Aaron Conole <aconole@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: David Marchand <david.marchand@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Wan Junjie <wanjunjie@bytedance.com>
Signed-off-by: Alin-Gabriel Serdean <aserdean@ovn.org>
cve_desc: A memory leak was found in Open vSwitch (OVS) during userspace IP fragmentation processing. An attacker could use this flaw to potentially exhaust available memory by keeping sending packet fragments.

commit_message:
Fix segmentation fault in shape inference logic.

When running shape functions, some functions (such as `MutableHashTableShape`)
produce extra output information in the form of a `ShapeAndType` struct.  The
shapes embedded in this struct are owned by an inference context that is
cleaned up almost immediately; if the upstream code attempts to access this
shape information, it can trigger a segfault.

`ShapeRefiner` is mitigating this for normal output shapes by cloning them
(and thus putting the newly created shape under ownership of an inference
context that will not die), but we were not doing the same for shapes and
types.  This commit fixes that by doing similar logic on output shapes and
types.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 384761124
Change-Id: I07c0c42d29dfbb55bfa13ec1f09ef825fb0a1a1d
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions when running shape functions, some functions (such as `MutableHashTableShape`) produce extra output information in the form of a `ShapeAndType` struct. The shapes embedded in this struct are owned by an inference context that is cleaned up almost immediately; if the upstream code attempts to access this shape information, it can trigger a segfault. `ShapeRefiner` is mitigating this for normal output shapes by cloning them (and thus putting the newly created shape under ownership of an inference context that will not die), but we were not doing the same for shapes and types. This commit fixes that by doing similar logic on output shapes and types. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit ee119d4a498979525046fba1c3dd3f13a039fbb1. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
swtpm: Check header size indicator against expected size (CID 375869)

This fix addresses Coverity issue CID 375869.

Check the header size indicated in the header of the state against the
expected size and return an error code in case the header size indicator
is different. There was only one header size so far since blobheader was
introduced, so we don't need to deal with different sizes.

Without this fix a specially craft header could have cause out-of-bounds
accesses on the byte array containing the swtpm's state.

Signed-off-by: Stefan Berger <stefanb@linux.ibm.com>
cve_desc: swtpm is a libtpms-based TPM emulator with socket, character device, and Linux CUSE interface. Versions prior to 0.5.3, 0.6.2, and 0.7.1 are vulnerable to out-of-bounds read. A specially crafted header of swtpm's state, where the blobheader's hdrsize indicator has an invalid value, may cause an out-of-bounds access when the byte array representing the state of the TPM is accessed. This will likely crash swtpm or prevent it from starting since the state cannot be understood. Users should upgrade to swtpm v0.5.3, v0.6.2, or v0.7.1 to receive a patch. There are currently no known workarounds.

1. The function `get_one_sourceline` reads a line from a source (either a buffer or a file) and handles line endings (DOS vs Unix) and escape sequences.

2. There is a specific check for trailing Ctrl-Z (which is a control character, ASCII 26) in DOS mode:
   ```c
   if (   (len == 1 || (len >= 2 && buf[len - 2] == '\n'))
        && sp->fileformat == EOL_DOS
        && buf[len - 1] == Ctrl_Z)
   {
       buf[len - 1] = NUL;
       break;
   }
   ```

   This code breaks the loop (i.e., terminates the line reading) if:
   - The line length is 1 OR (the line length is at least 2 and the second last character is a newline)
   - The file format is set to EOL_DOS (DOS line endings)
   - The last character is Ctrl-Z (which is a control character, not a typical text character)

3. The problem: In some contexts (like certain text files or binary files), Ctrl-Z might be a legitimate character in the data (for example, in some text files that use Ctrl-Z as a marker for end-of-file in Windows, or in files that contain control characters). If the code interprets a Ctrl-Z that is not intended as a line terminator (i.e., it's part of the data) as a line terminator, it will break the line reading prematurely.

4. The author's explanation mentions: "The handling of Ctrl-Z as a possible end-of-file marker in DOS is a bit niche but makes sense for some file formats." However, the code does not have a context check to ensure that the Ctrl-Z is actually a line terminator (e.g., it's the last character of a line and the file is in DOS format). Without such a check, the code might break on a Ctrl-Z that is not intended to be a line terminator.

5. This is a classic vulnerability: **misinterpretation of control characters as line terminators**. It can lead to:
   - Premature termination of line reading (if the file contains Ctrl-Z in the middle of a line)
   - Incomplete lines being returned (if the function breaks too early)
   - Potential for security issues if the source file is maliciously crafted to contain Ctrl-Z in the data (though in practice, this is less common for text files, but still a risk)

6. The code does not have a check to ensure that the Ctrl-Z is only processed when it is the last character of a line and the file is in DOS format.    - The growarray handling is efficient and the code has checks for buffer exhaustion, so it's not a critical vulnerability.

commit_message:
Fix FPE issue with `tf.raw_ops.Reverse`.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 371176973
Change-Id: Ic6d483bfc95313ec2299c2d1c956cfe96c96626c
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can cause a denial of service via a FPE runtime error in `tf.raw_ops.Reverse`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/36229ea9e9451dac14a8b1f4711c435a1d84a594/tensorflow/core/kernels/reverse_op.cc#L75-L76) performs a division based on the first dimension of the tensor argument. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

2. It checks if the input is a scalar (rank 0) and returns it without processing.

commit_message: Fix for CVE-2015-2141. Thanks to Evgeny Sidorov for reporting. Squaring to satisfy Jacobi requirements suggested by JPM.
cve_desc: The InvertibleRWFunction::CalculateInverse function in rw.cpp in libcrypt++ 5.6.2 does not properly blind private key operations for the Rabin-Williams digital signature algorithm, which allows remote attackers to obtain private keys via a timing attack.
reasoning:
Let me carefully analyze the code and the author's explanation to identify vulnerabilities.

The code is for an `InvertibleRWFunction::CalculateInverse` method that computes the inverse of a function (likely a square root operation in a cryptographic context). The function uses a probabilistic approach with random numbers to find a square root modulo a composite number.

Key parts of the code:
1. Generates a random r (coprime to m_n) using a loop
2. Computes re = (r^2 * x) mod m_n
3. Splits re into residues mod m_p and m_q
4. Checks if Jacobi symbols multiply to 1 (quadratic residue condition)
5. Adjusts residues if needed (the questionable part)
6. Computes square roots using parallel sections
7. Combines via CRT and unblinds
8. Verifies the result

The author's explanation indicates this is designed to find square roots (since it's called "CalculateInverse" for a function that squares).

The most critical vulnerability I see is in the adjustment step:

```cpp
if (Jacobi(cp, m_p) * Jacobi(cq, m_q) != 1)
{
    cp = cp.IsOdd() ? (cp+m_p) >> 1 : cp >> 1;
    cq = cq.IsOdd() ? (cq+m_q) >> 1 : cq >> 1;
}
```

This adjustment logic is non-standard and potentially incorrect. The Jacobi symbol product being -1 means one residue is a quadratic residue and the other is not. The adjustment step adds the modulus and shifts right (divides by 2), but this doesn't guarantee the result becomes a quadratic residue.

In my earlier example with m_p=7, m_q=11, x=2, r=3:
- Initial residues: cp=4 (residue), cq=7 (non-residue)
- After adjustment: cp=2 (residue), cq=9 (residue)
- But the final result y=1 didn't satisfy y^2 = x (1^2=1 ≠ 2)

This shows the adjustment step doesn't always work correctly. However, the code has a final verification step that checks if ApplyFunction(y) equals x and throws an exception if not. This is a good mitigation because it catches incorrect results.

The vulnerability is that the adjustment logic might produce incorrect residues, but the code's verification step mitigates this risk by ensuring only correct results are accepted.

We are given a code snippet and the author's explanation. As a Security Analyst, I must identify vulnerabilities.

Key points from the code and explanation:

1. The function `parse_die` processes attributes of a DWARF DIE (Debug Information Entry).
2. The loop runs for `i = 0` to `abbrev->count - 2` (i.e., `abbrev->count - 1` iterations).

Critical vulnerability:
- In DWARF, the abbreviation table (`abbrev`) contains definitions for attribute types (e.g., DW_AT_name, DW_AT_comp_dir). The number of entries in this table (`abbrev->count`) is fixed for the entire debug information.
- However, a single DIE (Debug Information Entry) has a variable number of attributes (as defined by the DIE's structure). The correct way to process a DIE is to first read the number of attributes in that DIE (from the DIE header) and then loop that many times.
- The current code loops over `abbrev->count - 1` (the size of the abbreviation table) instead of the actual number of attributes in the DIE. This is a fundamental design flaw.

Why is this a vulnerability?
- It can cause the function to process too many attributes (if `abbrev->count` is larger than the actual attributes in the DIE) or too few (if `abbrev->count` is smaller). This leads to:
  - Missing attributes (if the loop stops early) -> incorrect parsing of the DIE.
  - Processing invalid attributes (if the loop goes beyond the actual attributes) -> data corruption or crashes.
- The absence of a mechanism to read the actual attribute count from the DIE header (which is standard in DWARF) is a vulnerability because it breaks the expected parsing behavior.

Okay, let's try to figure out what this code does. So, the function is called afra_box_read, which is part of the ISOM (ISO Base Media File Format) library, probably for handling the Adobe Fragment Random Access box.

First, looking at the function signature: it takes a GF_Box pointer s and a GF_BitStream *bs. The GF_Box is a structure that represents a box in the file, and GF_BitStream is for reading bits from the file.

The code starts by casting s to GF_AdobeFragRandomAccessBox *ptr. That's the structure for the Adobe Fragment Random Access box. Then there's ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, 9). I remember that in ISOM, ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is a macro that adjusts the size of the box by subtracting the size of the header. The 9 here probably refers to the size of the box header (like 4 bytes for the box type and 4 for the size, but maybe 9 here is specific to this box).

Next, it reads several integers from the bitstream. The first one is ptr->long_ids, which is a 1-bit value. Then long_offsets (1-bit), global_entries (1-bit), reserved (5 bits), time_scale (32-bit unsigned). Then entry_count (32-bit unsigned).

Wait, the code checks if ptr->size / ( (ptr->long_offsets ? 16 : 12) ) < ptr->entry_count. Hmm. The size here is the size of the box. The denominator is 16 if long_offsets is 1, else 12. So it's checking if the total size of the box (after the header) is sufficient to hold the entry_count entries. Each entry is 16 bytes if long_offsets is set, else 12 bytes. So this is a sanity check to prevent reading past the end of the box.

Then it loops over entry_count times. For each entry, it allocates a GF_AfraEntry. Then it reads the time (64-bit) and the offset. If long_offsets is set, it reads 8 bytes (64-bit) for the offset; otherwise, 4 bytes (32-bit). Then it inserts the entry into ptr->local_access_entries.

After that, if global_entries is set (1-bit), it reads global_entry_count (32-bit). Then for each global entry, it allocates a GF_GlobalAfraEntry. Then reads time (64-bit), and depending on long_ids (1-bit), it reads segment and fragment as 32-bit or 16-bit. Then, depending on long_offsets, it reads afra_offset and offset_from_afra as 64-bit or 32-bit.

The function returns GF_OK on success, or error codes like GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE, GF_OUT_OF_MEM.

Fix tf.raw_ops.StagePeek vulnerability with invalid `index`.

Check that input is actually a scalar before treating it as such.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 445524908

Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.StagePeek` does not fully validate the input arguments. This results in a `CHECK`-failure which can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. The code assumes `index` is a scalar but there is no validation for this before accessing its value. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

Fix heap buffer overflow in stl_update_connects_remove_1


- Add argument value check to the stl_update_connects_remove_1
- Add neighbor value check in stl_remove_degenerate

Fixes https://github.com/admesh/admesh/issues/28
Merges https://github.com/admesh/admesh/pull/55

Fix heap OOB in `tf.raw_ops.RaggedGather`

PiperOrigin-RevId: 388355464
Change-Id: If14d96231d1cd7aad7c4d1c22c1bab1576b75717
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions if the arguments to `tf.raw_ops.RaggedGather` don't determine a valid ragged tensor code can trigger a read from outside of bounds of heap allocated buffers. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/8d72537c6abf5a44103b57b9c2e22c14f5f49698/tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_gather_op.cc#L70) directly reads the first dimension of a tensor shape before checking that said tensor has rank of at least 1 (i.e., it is not a scalar). Furthermore, the implementation does not check that the list given by `params_nested_splits` is not an empty list of tensors. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit a2b743f6017d7b97af1fe49087ae15f0ac634373. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
KVM: nSVM: always intercept VMLOAD/VMSAVE when nested (CVE-2021-3656)

If L1 disables VMLOAD/VMSAVE intercepts, and doesn't enable
Virtual VMLOAD/VMSAVE (currently not supported for the nested hypervisor),
then VMLOAD/VMSAVE must operate on the L1 physical memory, which is only
possible by making L0 intercept these instructions.

Failure to do so allowed the nested guest to run VMLOAD/VMSAVE unintercepted,
and thus read/write portions of the host physical memory.

Fixes: 89c8a4984fc9 ("KVM: SVM: Enable Virtual VMLOAD VMSAVE feature")

Suggested-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Maxim Levitsky <mlevitsk@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
cve_desc: A flaw was found in the KVM's AMD code for supporting SVM nested virtualization. The flaw occurs when processing the VMCB (virtual machine control block) provided by the L1 guest to spawn/handle a nested guest (L2). Due to improper validation of the "virt_ext" field, this issue could allow a malicious L1 to disable both VMLOAD/VMSAVE intercepts and VLS (Virtual VMLOAD/VMSAVE) for the L2 guest. As a result, the L2 guest would be allowed to read/write physical pages of the host, resulting in a crash of the entire system, leak of sensitive data or potential guest-to-host escape.

   - The code does `unlink(local.sun_path)` but does not check the return value.

   - This could lead to unexpected behavior (e.g., the bind failing) and might be a denial-of-service if the path is a directory.

- The author correctly notes that unlinking the path before binding is a good practice to handle existing files (from previous runs).

commit_message:
Fix overflow CHECK issue with `tf.raw_ops.UnsortedSegmentJoin`.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370766155
Change-Id: I33e7c6626224e1060a8a4ab51ad5d861c6d4c63e
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can cause a denial of service by controlling the values of `num_segments` tensor argument for `UnsortedSegmentJoin`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/a2a607db15c7cd01d754d37e5448d72a13491bdb/tensorflow/core/kernels/unsorted_segment_join_op.cc#L92-L93) assumes that the `num_segments` tensor is a valid scalar. Since the tensor is empty the `CHECK` involved in `.scalar<T>()()` that checks that the number of elements is exactly 1 will be invalidated and this would result in process termination. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.
reasoning:
We are reviewing the code for potential vulnerabilities. The problem states: "When in doubt, err on the side of caution and consider code vulnerable." Also, "The absence of security measures is often itself a vulnerability."

Let's break down the code:

1. The code processes three inputs: `input` (tensor of strings), `segment_id` (tensor of indices), and `num_segments_tensor` (scalar).

2. It checks:
   - `segment_dims != 0` (to avoid rank 0)
   - `segment_dims <= input_dims`
   - For each dimension i, `segment_id_shape.dim_size(i) == input_shape.dim_size(i)`
   - Segment IDs are in [0, num_segments)

3. It then creates an output tensor and processes the input and segment_id tensors.

The critical part is the nested loops that compute offsets and append to the output. The code uses:
- `big_stride` and `small_stride` from `GetStrides`
- `relative_offset_set` from `GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets`

Potential vulnerabilities:

1. **Out-of-bounds access**: The code does not explicitly check that the computed `offset` (for the input) is within the bounds of the input tensor. The `flat_input(offset)` could cause an out-of-bounds access if `offset` is negative or >= `flat_input.size()`.

   Why is this a vulnerability?
   - The code does not validate `offset` before accessing `flat_input(offset)`.
   - The `relative_offset_set` is generated by `GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets`, which might return offsets that are out of bounds if the helper functions are flawed.

2. **Incorrect stride calculation**: The helper functions `GetStrides` and `GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets` are critical. If they are implemented incorrectly (e.g., for multi-dimensional tensors), the code could access invalid memory. This is a common issue in tensor operations.

3. **Inefficient loops**: The nested loops (over `start_offset` and `relative_offset_set`) could be inefficient for large tensors, but this is more of a performance issue than a security vulnerability.

4. **No bounds check on `offset`**: The code does not check that `offset` is within the valid range of the input tensor. The `flat_input` is a flat view of the input tensor, so `offset` must be in [0, input_flat.size()).

commit_message:
xfrm: policy: check policy direction value

The 'dir' parameter in xfrm_migrate() is a user-controlled byte which is used
as an array index. This can lead to an out-of-bound access, kernel lockup and
DoS. Add a check for the 'dir' value.

This fixes CVE-2017-11600.

References: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1474928
Fixes: 80c9abaabf42 ("[XFRM]: Extension for dynamic update of endpoint address(es)")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v2.6.21-rc1
Reported-by: "bo Zhang" <zhangbo5891001@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Vladis Dronov <vdronov@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
cve_desc: net/xfrm/xfrm_policy.c in the Linux kernel through 4.12.3, when CONFIG_XFRM_MIGRATE is enabled, does not ensure that the dir value of xfrm_userpolicy_id is XFRM_POLICY_MAX or less, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via an XFRM_MSG_MIGRATE xfrm Netlink message.

commit_message:
cgroup-v1: Require capabilities to set release_agent

The cgroup release_agent is called with call_usermodehelper.  The function
call_usermodehelper starts the release_agent with a full set fo capabilities.
Therefore require capabilities when setting the release_agaent.

Reported-by: Tabitha Sable <tabitha.c.sable@gmail.com>
Tested-by: Tabitha Sable <tabitha.c.sable@gmail.com>
Fixes: 81a6a5cdd2c5 ("Task Control Groups: automatic userspace notification of idle cgroups")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v2.6.24+
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
Signed-off-by: Tejun Heo <tj@kernel.org>
cve_desc: A vulnerability was found in the Linux kernel’s cgroup_release_agent_write in the kernel/cgroup/cgroup-v1.c function. This flaw, under certain circumstances, allows the use of the cgroups v1 release_agent feature to escalate privileges and bypass the namespace isolation unexpectedly.

commit_message:
Fix a bug when getting a gzip header extra field with inflate().

If the extra field was larger than the space the user provided with
inflateGetHeader(), and if multiple calls of inflate() delivered
the extra header data, then there could be a buffer overflow of the
provided space. This commit assures that provided space is not
exceeded.
cve_desc: zlib through 1.2.12 has a heap-based buffer over-read or buffer overflow in inflate in inflate.c via a large gzip header extra field. NOTE: only applications that call inflateGetHeader are affected. Some common applications bundle the affected zlib source code but may be unable to call inflateGetHeader (e.g., see the nodejs/node reference).

commit_message:
HID: elo: fix memory leak in elo_probe

When hid_parse() in elo_probe() fails, it forgets to call usb_put_dev to
decrease the refcount.

Fix this by adding usb_put_dev() in the error handling code of elo_probe().

Fixes: fbf42729d0e9 ("HID: elo: update the reference count of the usb device structure")
Reported-by: syzkaller <syzkaller@googlegroups.com>
Signed-off-by: Dongliang Mu <mudongliangabcd@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
cve_desc: In drivers/hid/hid-elo.c in the Linux kernel before 5.16.11, a memory leak exists for a certain hid_parse error condition.

commit_message:
Fix a null pointer exception caused by branching on uninitialized data.

This is due to not checking that the params for the quantization exists. If there is no quantization, we should not access the `.params` field.

cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions all TFLite operations that use quantization can be made to use unitialized values. [For example](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/depthwise_conv.cc#L198-L200). commit_message:
libpq: reject extraneous data after SSL or GSS encryption handshake.

libpq collects up to a bufferload of data whenever it reads data from
the socket.  When SSL or GSS encryption is requested during startup,
any additional data received with the server's yes-or-no reply
remained in the buffer, and would be treated as already-decrypted data
once the encryption handshake completed.  Thus, a man-in-the-middle
with the ability to inject data into the TCP connection could stuff
some cleartext data into the start of a supposedly encryption-protected
database session.

This could probably be abused to inject faked responses to the
client's first few queries, although other details of libpq's behavior
make that harder than it sounds.  A different line of attack is to
exfiltrate the client's password, or other sensitive data that might
be sent early in the session.  That has been shown to be possible with
a server vulnerable to CVE-2021-23214.

To fix, throw a protocol-violation error if the internal buffer
is not empty after the encryption handshake.

Our thanks to Jacob Champion for reporting this problem.

Security: CVE-2021-23222

Bug 701785: fixed sanitizer heap-buffer-overflow in lprn_is_black().

In contrib/lips4/gdevlprn.c:lprn_is_black(), it seems that bpl is not
necessarily a multiple of lprn->nBw, so we need to explicitly avoid straying
into the next line's data.

This also avoids accessing beyond our buffer if we are already on the last
line, and so fixes the sanitizer error.

Fixes:
    ./sanbin/gs -sOutputFile=tmp -sDEVICE=lips2p ../bug-701785.pdf
cve_desc: A buffer overflow vulnerability in lprn_is_black() in contrib/lips4/gdevlprn.c of Artifex Software GhostScript v9.50 allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via a crafted PDF file. This is fixed in v9.51.

1. The function `lprn_is_black` checks if a region (starting at row `r`, height `h`, starting at column `bx`) is all black (by checking for non-zero pixels).

2. The critical calculation: `y0 = (r + h - bh) % maxY`
   - `maxY = lprn->BlockLine / lprn->nBh * lprn->nBh` (a multiple of `bh`)
   - `bh` is the block height (nBh)

3. The loop runs for `y` from 0 to `bh-1` (so `bh` lines) and accesses:
   `p = &lprn->ImageBuf[(y0 + y) * bpl + bx * lprn->nBw]`

4. **Vulnerability Analysis**:
   - The buffer `lprn->ImageBuf` is designed to hold `maxY` lines (each line is `bpl` bytes).
   - `y0` is computed modulo `maxY`, so `y0` is in `[0, maxY-1]`.
   - However, the loop accesses `y0 + y` for `y` in `[0, bh-1]`. The maximum index is `(maxY - 1) + (bh - 1)`.
   - Since `maxY` is a multiple of `bh` (let `maxY = k * bh`), then:
        `(maxY - 1) + (bh - 1) = k*bh - 1 + bh - 1 = (k+1)*bh - 2`
   - The buffer only has `maxY = k*bh` lines. Therefore, the access `(y0 + y)` can be as large as `(k+1)*bh - 2`, which is **beyond** the buffer's line count (which is `k*bh`).
   - This leads to **out-of-bounds access** to the `ImageBuf` buffer, which is a buffer overflow vulnerability.

5. **Why is this a vulnerability?**
   - The code does not check if `y0 + y` is within `[0, maxY-1]`. It assumes the modulo operation keeps the index in bounds, but the modulo operation only applies to `y0` (the starting line), not to the entire range `y0` to `y0 + bh - 1`.
   - This can cause the program to read/writing to memory outside the allocated buffer, leading to crashes, data corruption, or security exploits (e.g., arbitrary code execution).

   - High: The calculation of `y0` is modulo `maxY`, but the loop runs `bh` iterations (which is larger than the modulo adjustment). The buffer size is `maxY` lines, and the access goes beyond that. This is a classic buffer overflow pattern.

commit_message:
Bug 790784 - (CVE-2017-17784) heap overread in gbr parser / load_image.

We were assuming the input name was well formed, hence was
nul-terminated. As any data coming from external input, this has to be
thorougly checked.
Similar to commit 06d24a79af94837d615d0024916bb95a01bf3c59 but adapted
to older gimp-2-8 code.
cve_desc: In GIMP 2.8.22, there is a heap-based buffer over-read in load_image in plug-ins/common/file-gbr.c in the gbr import parser, related to mishandling of UTF-8 data.

discussion.author_submission:
We are given a function `load_image` that is part of a GIMP (GNU Image Manipulation Program) plugin or module. The function is designed to load a GIMP brush file (which is a special file format for brushes) and convert it into a GIMP image (with a single layer) that can be used in the image editing software.

Let's break down the intent and design choices:

### Intent
The function reads a brush file (which is a binary file) and converts it into a GIMP image. The brush file is expected to have a specific header (the `BrushHeader` structure) that describes the image dimensions and the data format. The function then:
1. Opens the file in binary mode.
2. Reads the header and converts the network byte order (big-endian) to host byte order (using `g_ntohl`).
3. Validates the header (ensuring dimensions are within bounds, and the byte count per pixel is one of the supported values: 1, 2, 4, or 18).
4. Handles different versions of the brush format (version 1, 2, 3) and possibly a pattern header (for backward compatibility with old .gpb files).
5. Reads the actual brush data (the pixel data) and converts it to the appropriate format (if necessary) for GIMP.
6. Creates a new GIMP image with the brush data as a layer, and attaches the brush name as a parasite (a persistent data structure in GIMP).
7. Finally, it sets up the pixel region and copies the brush data into the layer.

### Design Choices

1. **Byte Order Handling**: The function uses `g_ntohl` (network to host long) to convert the header fields from network byte order (big-endian) to host byte order. This is a standard practice for cross-platform binary file reading.

2. **Header Validation**: The function checks the header for:
   - Non-zero and within `GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` for width and height.
   - The `bytes` field (per pixel) must be 1, 2, 4, or 18 (for a specific float format).
   - A sanity check on the total size: `G_MAXSIZE / (bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes) >= 1` (to avoid overflow).

3. **Version Handling**:
   - **Version 1**: The function adjusts the `bh.spacing` to 25 and rewinds the file by 8 bytes (to skip the missing magic number and spacing). This is for backward compatibility with older brush files that didn't have the magic number and spacing.
   - **Version 3**: Handles the "cinepaint" brush format. If the brush uses 18 bytes (which is a float16 format), it converts it to 2 bytes (for float32? but note: 18 bytes per brush? Actually, the comment says "FLOAT16_GRAY_GIMAGE", so it's a 16-bit float per channel? But the code sets `bh.bytes=2` meaning 2 bytes per pixel? This is a bit confusing. However, the code then proceeds as if it's 2 bytes per pixel. The comment says: "cinepaint brush" and the 18 bytes might be a specific format that the code converts to 2 bytes per pixel for the purpose of the brush).
   - **Version 2**: Checks for a specific magic number and header size to be valid. If not, it falls through to the default (which is an unsupported format).
   - **Default**: Prints a message and returns an error.

4. **Reading the Brush Name**: After the header, there is a block of data (of size `bh.header_size - sizeof(BrushHeader)`) that is read as a string (UTF-8). If this block is empty, it uses "Unnamed". This name is then stored as a parasite in the image.

5. **Handling Pattern Header (for backward compatibility)**: The function checks if the brush file has a pattern header (for old .gpb files). If so, it reads the pattern header and then converts the brush data to 4 bytes per pixel (RGBA) by reading the pattern data (which is 3 bytes per pixel) and then converting each 3-byte value to a 4-byte value (with an alpha channel set to the original value). This is a complex conversion and is done only for the case of 1-byte brush data (which is grayscale) and when the pattern header is present.

6. **Data Conversion**:
   - For `bh.bytes = 2` (16-bit floats): The function converts each 16-bit float to an 8-bit integer (by scaling to 0-255). It does this by reading the 16-bit value, converting it to a float, then scaling to 0-255. Note: The code uses a union to handle the byte order (it checks for little-endian vs big-endian). This is a common technique for converting between float and integer representations.
   - For `bh.bytes = 4` (32-bit floats): The function does not handle it directly (it's handled by the `case 4` in the switch for the image type). But note: the function does not convert 32-bit floats to 8-bit? Actually, the function only converts 16-bit floats to 8-bit. The 32-bit floats are not converted in this function (they are used as is for RGBA?).

7. **Image Creation**: The function creates a new image with the given dimensions and base type (gray for 1 byte, RGBA for 4 bytes). It then creates a layer and copies the brush data into the layer.

8. **Inversion for Grayscale**: If the image is grayscale (1 byte), it inverts the layer (this is a common operation for brushes in GIMP).

### Potential Risky Parts

1. **Memory Allocation and Freeing**: The function allocates memory for the brush data and the name. It is important to note that the function does not check for memory allocation failures (it uses `g_malloc` and `g_free`). However, the function does check for `read` failures and then frees the allocated memory. But note: if `g_malloc` fails, the function would return -1 without freeing (because it doesn't check the return value of `g_malloc`). This is a potential issue because if `g_malloc` fails, the function returns -1 and the caller might not know that the memory was allocated (but the function doesn't free it because it returns early). Actually, the function does:
   ```c
   brush_buf = g_malloc (size);
   if (read (fd, brush_buf, size) != size)
   {
     close (fd);
     g_free (brush_buf);
     g_free (name);
     return -1;
   }

Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.SparseTensorDenseAdd` does not fully validate the input arguments. In this case, a reference gets bound to a `nullptr` during kernel execution. This is undefined behavior. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

patch 8.2.4151: reading beyond the end of a line

Problem:    Reading beyond the end of a line.
Solution:   For block insert only use the offset for correcting the length.

Okay, let's try to figure out what this code does. So, the function is called block_insert, and it's part of a text editor, probably Vim or something similar, given the variable names like State, ml_get, etc.

First, the function takes several parameters: oap (which is probably an operation argument), s (the string to insert), b_insert (a flag indicating whether it's an insert or append), and bdp (a block definition structure).

The main goal seems to be inserting or appending text into a block of lines. The code loops through each line in the block (from oap->start.lnum +1 to oap->end.lnum). For each line, it processes the insertion.

Let me break down the steps:

1. It sets State to INSERT to avoid REPLACE mode. That makes sense because when inserting, you don't want the state to be replace.

2. It calculates the length of the string s (s_len).

3. Then, for each line number lnum in the range:

   a. Calls block_prep to prepare the block for this line.

   b. If bdp->is_short is true and b_insert is true, it skips the line. So, if the block is short and it's an insert operation, skip this line.

   c. Gets the old line (oldp) using ml_get.

   d. Depending on whether it's an insert (b_insert) or append:

      - For insert: sets ts_val to bdp->start_char_vcols (probably the visual column of the start character), spaces to bdp->startspaces (number of spaces before insertion?), and offset to bdp->textcol (the column where insertion starts).

      - For append: more complex. It calculates spaces as padding after the block. If the block isn't short, it might be adding spaces to align with the end of the block. If it's a tab, it handles that.

   e. Then, there's a part for multi-byte characters. If the text is in multi-byte (has_mbyte), it adjusts the spaces to avoid splitting multi-byte characters. For example, if inserting spaces, it checks where the current line starts and adjusts the offset to not cut a multi-byte character.

   f. Allocates new memory for the line (newp) with the size calculated as old line length + spaces + s_len + some extra for tabs (ts_val - spaces) + count (which is related to tabs) + 1 (for null terminator).

   g. Copies the part of the line before the insertion point (up to offset) to newp.

   h. Inserts spaces (if spaces >0) after the copied part.

   i. Copies the new string s into newp.

   j. Then, if there are spaces and it's not a short block, checks if the next character is a tab. If so, it inserts more spaces (ts_val - spaces) and increments count (which tracks how many tabs are being split).

   k. Adjusts the offset and copies the rest of the old line.

   l. Replaces the line with the newp.

   m. If it's an insert, it updates the text properties (inserted_bytes).

   n. If it's the last line (lnum == oap->end.lnum), it sets the end mark (curbuf->b_op_end) to the end of the block.

4. After processing all lines, it calls changed_lines to mark the lines as changed.

So, the main intent here is to insert or append text into a block of lines, handling tabs, multi-byte characters, and alignment.

Design choices:

- Using a loop over each line in the block. This is efficient for block operations.

- Handling tabs by inserting spaces (ts_val) which is the visual column of a tab. So, when inserting a tab, it's replaced by spaces to maintain the visual width.

- The multi-byte handling: it checks the start of the line to avoid splitting multi-byte characters. For example, if inserting spaces, it ensures that the offset doesn't cut a multi-byte character.

- The count variable tracks how many extra spaces are needed when splitting a tab. For example, if a tab is split into spaces, count is incremented by the number of spaces (ts_val - 1).

1. **Memory allocation**: The allocation size is calculated as STRLEN(oldp) + spaces + s_len + (spaces >0 && !bdp->is_short ? ts_val - spaces : 0) + count +1. If this calculation is incorrect, it could lead to buffer overflows. For example, if the string is very long, or if the spaces and ts_val are miscalculated.

2. **Multi-byte handling**: The code uses (*mb_head_off) to get the start of a multi-byte character. If this function is not correctly implemented, it could lead to incorrect offsets. For example, if the function returns a value that's not the correct number of bytes, the offset could be off.

3. **Tab handling**: When inserting a tab, it's replaced by spaces. But if the tab is split (e.g., the insertion point is in the middle of a tab), the code inserts spaces and increments count. However, the count is used in the allocation and copying. If the count is miscalculated, it could lead to incorrect memory usage.

4. **Edge cases**: For example, when spaces is negative (spaces <0), it's set to 0. But why would spaces be negative? Maybe due to cursor movement. The code handles it by setting to 0, which might be a safe check.

5. **The 'is_short' flag**: If the block is short and it's an insert, it skips the line. This might be a way to handle blocks that are short (like a single line) but the code might not handle all cases correctly.

commit_message:
Prevent null pointer dereference in `mutable_graph_view`

Change-Id: I577eb9d9ac470fcec0501423171e739a4ec0cb5c
cve_desc: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. Under certain scenarios, Grappler component of TensorFlow can trigger a null pointer dereference. There are 2 places where this can occur, for the same malicious alteration of a `SavedModel` file (fixing the first one would trigger the same dereference in the second place). First, during constant folding, the `GraphDef` might not have the required nodes for the binary operation. If a node is missing, the correposning `mul_*child` would be null, and the dereference in the subsequent line would be incorrect. We have a similar issue during `IsIdentityConsumingSwitch`. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

Let me analyze the code:

Original Code:
```cpp
bool IsIdentityConsumingSwitch(const MutableGraphView& graph,
                               const NodeDef& node) {
  if ((IsIdentity(node) || IsIdentityNSingleInput(node)) &&
      node.input_size() > 0) {
    TensorId tensor_id = ParseTensorName(node.input(0));
    if (IsTensorIdControlling(tensor_id)) {
      return false;
    }

    NodeDef* input_node = graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node());
    return IsSwitch(*input_node);
  }
  return false;
}
```

Author's Explanation: (as provided)

Key points from the code and explanation:
1. The function checks if the node is an Identity or IdentityNSingleInput and has at least one input.
2. It parses the first input's tensor name to get a TensorId.
3. It checks if this TensorId is controlling (a control input) and returns false if so.
4. Then it gets the input node from the graph and checks if it's a Switch node.

Potential vulnerabilities:

1. **Null pointer dereference**: 
   - `graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node())` returns a `NodeDef*` which could be null. 
   - The code then dereferences `*input_node` (i.e., `IsSwitch(*input_node)`) without checking if `input_node` is null. 
   - This is a classic null pointer dereference vulnerability. If the node does not exist in the graph, the program will crash.

2. **Invalid tensor name**:
   - `ParseTensorName(node.input(0))` might crash if `node.input(0)` is an invalid tensor name (e.g., empty string, malformed name). 
   - The code does not validate the input name before parsing.

3. **Assumption about input size**:
   - The code checks `node.input_size() > 0` but does not handle the case where the input name is invalid (which could be caught by the ParseTensorName call). However, the main issue is the crash in ParseTensorName.

4. **Control input handling**:
   - The code checks `IsTensorIdControlling` and returns false if true. This is a good practice to avoid control inputs (which are not regular nodes). This is not a vulnerability but a security measure.

1. **Null pointer dereference when input node is not found**:

   - Description: The code dereferences `*input_node` without checking if `graph.GetNode()` returns a null pointer.

2. **Invalid tensor name causing ParseTensorName to crash**:
   - Type: "Invalid Input Handling"
   - Description: The code passes `node.input(0)` directly to `ParseTensorName` without validation, which may crash on invalid names.

Confidence: 
- For both, we have high confidence because null pointer dereferences and invalid input parsing are common and well-known issues. The code does not have any checks for these cases.

cve_desc: An unauthenticated stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability in common.c's handle_PORT in uftpd FTP server versions 2.10 and earlier can be abused to cause a crash and could potentially lead to remote code execution.

The problem states: "When in doubt, err on the side of caution and consider code vulnerable." Also, "The absence of security measures is often itself a vulnerability."

Let me analyze the code:

The function `handle_PORT` processes an FTP PORT command. The client sends a string with six numbers (IP octets and port split into two bytes). The code:
1. Cleans up previous data socket if exists.
2. Parses the string into six integers (a, b, c, d, e, f) using `sscanf`.
3. Formats the IP address as a string (a.b.c.d).
4. Checks the IP address with `inet_aton` (if invalid, returns error).
5. Copies the IP string and sets the port as `e * 256 + f`.
6. Sends a success message.

Potential vulnerabilities:

1. **Unvalidated sscanf parse count**: The code uses `sscanf` without checking if all six numbers were successfully parsed. If the input string has fewer than six numbers (e.g., "1,2,3,4,5"), then `e` and `f` will be uninitialized (garbage values). This leads to a potentially invalid port number (e.g., `e` might be 5 and `f` might be 0, but if the input has only 5 numbers, `f` is uninitialized and could be any value). This is a vulnerability because it can lead to incorrect port numbers being used.

2. **Port range validation missing**: The code calculates the port as `e * 256 + f` but does not check if the result is within the valid 16-bit range (0-65535). For example, if `e=256` and `f=0`, the port becomes 65760 (which is invalid). This is a vulnerability because the server might attempt to connect to an invalid port.

3. **No input sanitization for non-numeric values**: The code uses `sscanf` to parse integers, but if the input contains non-numeric characters (e.g., "1,2,3,4,5,abc"), `sscanf` will fail to parse the last number and set `f` to 0 (or garbage). However, the code does not check for this failure. The `inet_aton` check would then fail (because the IP string would be "1.2.3.4" which is valid, but the port would be `e*256 + 0` which might be valid, but the input was invalid). Actually, the problem is that the port might be set to a garbage value if the input has non-numeric. But note: the code does not check the return value of `sscanf`. But in reality, if the input has non-numeric, `sscanf` will stop at the first non-numeric and leave the rest uninitialized. This could lead to a port value that is garbage. However, the code does not check for this. But the main issue is the unvalidated count (vulnerability 1) which covers this.

commit_message:
Unsquashfs: additional write outside destination directory exploit fix

An issue on github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
showed how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and '..') can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

Since then it has been shown that specially crafted Squashfs filesystems
that contain a symbolic link pointing outside of the destination directory,
coupled with an identically named file within the same directory, can
cause Unsquashfs to write files outside of the destination directory.

Specifically the symbolic link produces a pathname pointing outside
of the destination directory, which is then followed when writing the
duplicate identically named file within the directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by explictly checking for duplicate
filenames within a directory.  As directories in v2.1, v3.x, and v4.0
filesystems are sorted, this is achieved by checking for consecutively
identical filenames.  Additionally directories are checked to
ensure they are sorted, to avoid attempts to evade the duplicate
check.

Version 1.x and 2.0 filesystems (where the directories were unsorted)
are sorted and then the above duplicate filename check is applied.

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
cve_desc: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-2.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 allows Directory Traversal, a different vulnerability than CVE-2021-40153. A squashfs filesystem that has been crafted to include a symbolic link and then contents under the same filename in a filesystem can cause unsquashfs to first create the symbolic link pointing outside the expected directory, and then the subsequent write operation will cause the unsquashfs process to write through the symbolic link elsewhere in the filesystem.

commit_message:
Fixed frame allocation from an awaited frame.

njs_function_frame_save() is used to save the awaited frame when "await"
instruction is encountered. The saving was done as a memcpy() of
existing runtime frame.

njs_function_frame_alloc() is used to alloc a new function frame, this
function tries to use a spare preallocated memory from the previous
frame first.  Previously, this function might result in "use-after-free"
when invoked from a restored frame saved with njs_function_frame_save().
Because njs_function_frame_save() left pointers to the spare memory of
the original frame which may be already free when saved frame is
restored.

The fix is to erase fields for the spare memory from the saved frame.

This closes #469 issue on Github.

commit_message:
Unsquashfs: additional write outside destination directory exploit fix

An issue on github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
showed how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and '..') can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

Since then it has been shown that specially crafted Squashfs filesystems
that contain a symbolic link pointing outside of the destination directory,
coupled with an identically named file within the same directory, can
cause Unsquashfs to write files outside of the destination directory.

Specifically the symbolic link produces a pathname pointing outside
of the destination directory, which is then followed when writing the
duplicate identically named file within the directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by explictly checking for duplicate
filenames within a directory.  As directories in v2.1, v3.x, and v4.0
filesystems are sorted, this is achieved by checking for consecutively
identical filenames.  Additionally directories are checked to
ensure they are sorted, to avoid attempts to evade the duplicate
check.

Version 1.x and 2.0 filesystems (where the directories were unsorted)
are sorted and then the above duplicate filename check is applied.

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
cve_desc: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-2.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 allows Directory Traversal, a different vulnerability than CVE-2021-40153. A squashfs filesystem that has been crafted to include a symbolic link and then contents under the same filename in a filesystem can cause unsquashfs to first create the symbolic link pointing outside the expected directory, and then the subsequent write operation will cause the unsquashfs process to write through the symbolic link elsewhere in the filesystem.

Check that indices are non-negative. Fix several identical code sites.

cve_desc: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.EditDistance` has incomplete validation. Users can pass negative values to cause a segmentation fault based denial of service. In multiple places throughout the code, one may compute an index for a write operation. However, the existing validation only checks against the upper bound of the array. Hence, it is possible to write before the array by massaging the input to generate negative values for `loc`. commit_message:
Fix security vulnerability with LSTMBlockCellOp

PiperOrigin-RevId: 446028341
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.LSTMBlockCell` does not fully validate the input arguments. This results in a `CHECK`-failure which can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. The code does not validate the ranks of any of the arguments to this API call. This results in `CHECK`-failures when the elements of the tensor are accessed. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.LoadAndRemapMatrix does not fully validate the input arguments. We are given a function `extract_arg` that is part of a reverse engineering library (R2, Radare2). The function is designed to extract and handle arguments (or stack variables) from a disassembled function.

### Intent of the Function
The function `extract_arg` is intended to:
1. Identify a register that is used as an argument (or a stack variable) in the current instruction.
2. Determine the offset of the argument (or stack variable) relative to the stack frame (or base pointer).
3. Create a variable (if not already present) for that argument or stack variable and record the access (read/write) at the instruction address.

The function is called with:
- `anal`: the RAnal (analysis) context
- `fcn`: the function being analyzed
- `op`: the current instruction operation (RAnalOp)
- `reg`: the register name (e.g., "rbx", "rsp")
- `sign`: a character indicating the sign of the offset (either '+' or '-')
- `type`: a type indicator (e.g., R_ANAL_VAR_KIND_SPV for stack pointer variable)

### Design Choices and Flow

The function has two main branches: one for when `*sign` is '+' (which typically indicates an argument) and one for when it's '-' (which typically indicates a stack variable).

#### Step 1: Finding the register in the source operands
The function first loops through the source operands of the instruction to find a register that matches the given `reg` (the register we are interested in). If found, it checks the sign condition (if the delta is positive and `*sign` is '+' OR negative and `*sign` is '-'). If so, it sets `ptr` to the absolute value of the delta and breaks.

#### Step 2: If no register found, try to parse the ESIL expression
If the register wasn't found in the source operands, the function tries to parse the ESIL (Expression Syntax Intermediate Language) string of the instruction. It looks for the pattern: `",%s,%s,"` (where `%s` is the register and `sign`). Then it tries to extract the address (the part that is a number) from the ESIL string.

The function then tries to interpret the extracted string as a number (using `r_num_get`). If it's a number, it sets `ptr` to that number. There are several conditions that might cause it to skip (e.g., if the address is a stack pointer and the instruction is a push/pop, etc.) and then it goes to a label `beach` (which is a cleanup point).

#### Step 3: Handling the argument (if sign is '+')
If `*sign` is '+', then:
- It checks if the offset `ptr` is within the stack frame (for arguments). It computes `frame_off` (the offset from the base pointer or stack pointer).
- It checks if `frame_off` is within a safe range (maxstackframe).
- If there's an existing variable for that offset, it updates the access.
- Otherwise, it tries to generate a variable name (either by using the function's argument type or by auto-naming).
- It creates a new variable and sets the access.

#### Step 4: Handling the stack variable (if sign is '-')
If `*sign` is '-', then:
- It computes `frame_off` as `-(ptr + fcn->bp_off)`. This is because the stack frame is relative to the base pointer (bp).
- It checks the same range condition.
- If there's an existing variable, it updates the access.
- Otherwise, it creates a new variable (with a name) and sets the access.

1. **Inconsistent ESIL Parsing**: The function has a comment `//XXX: This is a workaround for inconsistent esil` and a block that checks for stack operations. This indicates that the ESIL parsing might be error-prone and the function is trying to handle cases where the analysis didn't set `op->stackop` (which is a flag for stack operations). This is a known issue in the library.

2. **Stack Frame Offsets**: The function uses `maxstackframe` (1024*8) to limit the stack frame. This is a hard limit and might be too small for some functions (e.g., large stack frames). However, it's a common practice to set a limit to avoid excessive memory usage.

3. **Variable Name Generation**: The function uses `r_anal_function_autoname_var` for variable names. This function might generate names that are not very descriptive (e.g., `var_0`, `var_1`). Also, there is a commented-out check that skips arguments beyond 48 (which might be a specific requirement for the library).

4. **Assumptions about the Stack**: The function assumes that the stack frame is set up with the base pointer (bp) and stack pointer (sp). This might not hold for all architectures (e.g., some architectures use different calling conventions). However, the function is designed for the common x86 and x64 architectures.

5. **Handling of Stack Operations**: The function has a block that checks for stack operations (push, pop, ret) and if the instruction is a stack operation and the address is a number, it skips (by going to `beach`). This is to avoid creating variables for stack operations (which are handled by the stack frame).

6. **The `beach` Label**: The function uses a label `beach` for cleanup (freeing the esil_buf). commit_message:
Prevent use after free in `DecodePng` kernel.

We are cleaning up the memory in `decode` and then we are using an `OP_REQUIRES` to check an invariant on the `decode` data.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 409299145
Change-Id: I4eb93aaca52483eb202e89b78df07fbb2f6cb254
cve_desc: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. A malicious user can cause a use after free behavior when decoding PNG images. After `png::CommonFreeDecode(&decode)` gets called, the values of `decode.width` and `decode.height` are in an unspecified state. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

const int width = static_cast<int>(decode.width);
const int height = static_cast<int>(decode.height);
const int64_t total_size = static_cast<int64_t>(width) * static_cast<int64_t>(height);
if (width != static_cast<int64_t>(decode.width) || width <= 0 ||
    width >= (1LL << 27) || height != static_cast<int64_t>(decode.height) ||
    height <= 0 || height >= (1LL << 27) || total_size >= (1LL << 29)) {
  png::CommonFreeDecode(&decode);
  OP_REQUIRES(context, false,
              errors::InvalidArgument("PNG size too large for int: ",
                                      decode.width, " by ", decode.height));
}
```

This code checks:
- That width/height don't overflow when cast to `int`
- That dimensions are positive
- That individual dimensions are less than 134 million (1<<27)

- Memory exhaustion from extremely large images
- Potential denial-of-service attacks from maliciously crafted PNG files

if (op_type_ == "DecodeBmp") {

patch 8.2.4215: illegal memory access when copying lines in Visual mode

Problem:    Illegal memory access when copying lines in Visual mode.
Solution:   Adjust the Visual position after copying lines.
cve_desc: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.

We are given a code snippet and the author's explanation. As a Security Analyst, I must identify vulnerabilities and output JSON with:
- vulnerability_detected (bool)
- vulnerabilities (array of vulnerability objects)
- reasoning (string)

The user says: "When in doubt, err on the side of caution and consider code vulnerable." Also, "The absence of security measures is often itself a vulnerability."

Let me analyze the code and the author's explanation.

The code is a function `ex_copy` in Vim (a text editor) that copies lines from `line1` to `line2` to a destination line `n`.

Key parts of the code:
1. Calculates `count = line2 - line1 + 1`.
2. Checks if `CMOD_LOCKMARKS` is not set and sets operation marks.
3. Calls `u_save(n, n+1)` which returns FAIL on error.
4. Sets cursor to `n`.
5. Loop from `line1` to `line2`:
   - Saves the line with `vim_strsave`
   - Appends the line to the current cursor line
   - Frees the saved string
   - If `line1 == n`, sets `line1` to `curwin->w_cursor.lnum`
   - Increments `line1`
   - If `curwin->w_cursor.lnum < line1`, increments `line1` again
   - Increments cursor line
6. Calls `appended_lines_mark` and prints the count.

The author's explanation describes the code as handling three situations (destination above, between, or below the source range) and the logic for skipping lines when the destination is within the source range.

Potential vulnerabilities:

1. **Incorrect line skipping leading to missing lines**: As analyzed in the thought process, when the destination `n` is between `line1` and `line2`, the code skips the last line of the source range. This is a logical error that causes fewer lines to be copied than expected. This is a vulnerability because it leads to incorrect behavior (a bug) that could be exploited by users to copy fewer lines than intended.

2. **Memory safety**: The code uses `vim_strsave` to save a line before appending. This is good practice to avoid modifying the line during the operation. However, if the line is extremely long, this could cause memory exhaustion. But in Vim, line lengths are typically constrained (e.g., by the editor's limits), so this might not be a critical vulnerability. However, the absence of a check for memory allocation failure in `vim_strsave` could be a problem. But note: `vim_strsave` is a Vim-specific function that is designed to handle memory safely (it returns NULL on failure). The code checks `if (p != NULL)`, so it handles the failure case. Therefore, this is not a vulnerability.

3. **Cursor position handling**: The code increments the cursor line after each append (`++curwin->w_cursor.lnum`). This might cause issues if the cursor is moved by other operations during the copy (e.g., if the buffer is modified). However, this function is part of the Vim command execution and is designed to run in a specific context (the current buffer). The code seems to handle the cursor movement correctly for the intended use case. This is not a clear vulnerability.

4. **Buffer modification during copy**: The code does not check if the buffer is being modified during the copy operation. If the buffer is changed (e.g., by another command), the copied lines might be incorrect. However, in Vim, the `ex_copy` function is typically called in a context where the buffer is not being modified (it's a command that runs in a controlled environment). This is a potential issue but not a critical vulnerability.

5. **Edge cases**: The code does not handle the case where `line1` or `line2` are out of bounds (e.g., negative, or beyond the buffer size). However, Vim typically validates line numbers in such functions. This is not a vulnerability per se.

The most critical vulnerability is the one we identified in point 1: incorrect line skipping when the destination is within the source range. This is a bug that leads to incorrect behavior (missing lines) and is a vulnerability because it can be exploited by users to get fewer lines than expected.

commit_message:
Prevent null dereference read in `GetInitOp`.

We have a map of maps. We test that the key exists in the first map but then we don't have any validation that this also means the second map has the needed key. In the scenarios where this is not the case, we'll dereference a nullptr, if we don't have this check

PiperOrigin-RevId: 408739325
Change-Id: If9bb7ed759aba1f3b56a34913f209508dbaf65ce
cve_desc: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `GetInitOp` is vulnerable to a crash caused by dereferencing a null pointer. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
grep -F: fix a heap buffer (read) overrun

grep's read buffer is often filled to its full size, except when
reading the final buffer of a file.  In that case, the number of
bytes read may be far less than the size of the buffer.  However, for
certain unusual pattern/text combinations, grep -F would mistakenly
examine bytes in that uninitialized region of memory when searching
for a match.  With carefully chosen inputs, one can cause grep -F to
read beyond the end of that buffer altogether.  This problem arose via
commit v2.18-90-g73893ff with the introduction of a more efficient
heuristic using what is now the memchr_kwset function. The use of
that function in bmexec_trans could leave TP much larger than EP,
and the subsequent call to bm_delta2_search would mistakenly access
beyond end of the main input read buffer.

* src/kwset.c (bmexec_trans): When TP reaches or exceeds EP,
do not call bm_delta2_search.
* tests/kwset-abuse: New file.
* tests/Makefile.am (TESTS): Add it.
* THANKS.in: Update.
* NEWS (Bug fixes): Mention it.

Prior to this patch, this command would trigger a UMR:

commit_message:
nfc: nfcmrvl: main: reorder destructive operations in nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev to avoid bugs

There are destructive operations such as nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort and
gpio_free in nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev. The resources such as firmware,
gpio and so on could be destructed while the upper layer functions such as
nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_start and nfcmrvl_nci_recv_frame is executing, which leads
to double-free, use-after-free and null-ptr-deref bugs.

There are three situations that could lead to double-free bugs.

The first situation is shown below:

   (Thread 1)                 |      (Thread 2)
nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_start         |
 ...                          |  nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev
 release_firmware()           |   nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort
  kfree(fw) //(1)             |    fw_dnld_over
                              |     release_firmware
  ...                         |      kfree(fw) //(2)
                              |     ...

The second situation is shown below:

   (Thread 1)                 |      (Thread 2)
nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_start         |
 ...                          |
 mod_timer                    |
 (wait a time)                |
 fw_dnld_timeout              |  nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev
   fw_dnld_over               |   nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort
    release_firmware          |    fw_dnld_over
     kfree(fw) //(1)          |     release_firmware
     ...                      |      kfree(fw) //(2)

The third situation is shown below:

       (Thread 1)               |       (Thread 2)
nfcmrvl_nci_recv_frame          |
 if(..->fw_download_in_progress)|
  nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_recv_frame    |
   queue_work                   |
                                |
fw_dnld_rx_work                 | nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev
 fw_dnld_over                   |  nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort
  release_firmware              |   fw_dnld_over
   kfree(fw) //(1)              |    release_firmware
                                |     kfree(fw) //(2)

The firmware struct is deallocated in position (1) and deallocated
in position (2) again.

The crash trace triggered by POC is like below:

BUG: KASAN: double-free or invalid-free in fw_dnld_over
Call Trace:
  kfree
  fw_dnld_over
  nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev
  nci_uart_tty_close
  tty_ldisc_kill
  tty_ldisc_hangup
  __tty_hangup.part.0
  tty_release
  ...

What's more, there are also use-after-free and null-ptr-deref bugs
in nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_start. If we deallocate firmware struct, gpio or
set null to the members of priv->fw_dnld in nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev,
then, we dereference firmware, gpio or the members of priv->fw_dnld in
nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_start, the UAF or NPD bugs will happen.

This patch reorders destructive operations after nci_unregister_device
in order to synchronize between cleanup routine and firmware download
routine.

The nci_unregister_device is well synchronized. If the device is
detaching, the firmware download routine will goto error. If firmware
download routine is executing, nci_unregister_device will wait until
firmware download routine is finished.

Fixes: 3194c6870158 ("NFC: nfcmrvl: add firmware download support")
Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
cve_desc: A flaw in Linux Kernel found in nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev() in drivers/nfc/nfcmrvl/main.c can lead to use after free both read or write when non synchronized between cleanup routine and firmware download routine.

The instructions say: "When in doubt, err on the side of caution and consider code vulnerable." Also, "The absence of security measures is often itself a vulnerability."

Let's analyze the code:

```c
void nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev(struct nfcmrvl_private *priv)
{
	struct nci_dev *ndev = priv->ndev;

	if (priv->ndev->nfc_dev->fw_download_in_progress)
		nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort(priv);

	nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit(priv);

	if (gpio_is_valid(priv->config.reset_n_io))
		gpio_free(priv->config.reset_n_io);

	nci_unregister_device(ndev);
	nci_free_device(ndev);
	kfree(priv);
}
```

Key observations:

1. **No error handling for NCI functions**: The code calls `nci_unregister_device` and `nci_free_device` without checking their return values. In a kernel context, if these functions fail (e.g., due to a race condition or invalid state), the cleanup might be incomplete. This could lead to resource leaks (e.g., the device structure not being properly freed) or inconsistent states (e.g., the device being left in a partially unregistered state). This is a critical vulnerability because the function is called during device unregistration, a critical cleanup phase.

2. **Assumption about firmware state**: The code checks `fw_download_in_progress` before aborting. However, if this flag is not accurately maintained (e.g., due to a race condition or incorrect state transition), it might abort a download that isn't actually in progress or miss an ongoing download. But the author's explanation states they assume the flag is correctly set, so this is less critical than the error handling issue.

3. **GPIO handling**: The code checks `gpio_is_valid` before freeing the GPIO. This is a good practice and not a vulnerability.

4. **Memory safety**: The code uses `kfree(priv)` at the end. This is safe because the function is called during unregistration, so `priv` should be valid and allocated. There's no double-free risk because the function is called once per device.

5. **Order of operations**: The order (abort firmware -> deinit firmware -> free GPIO -> unregister) is logical and follows standard cleanup practices.

In kernel device unregistration, failure to handle errors from these functions can cause resource leaks (e.g., device structures not properly freed) or inconsistent states (e.g., device left in partially unregistered state). commit_message: Pull request: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/pull/4963
cve_desc: A vulnerability was found in ImageMagick, causing an outside the range of representable values of type 'unsigned char' at coders/psd.c, when crafted or untrusted input is processed. This leads to a negative impact to application availability or other problems related to undefined behavior.
reasoning:
We are reviewing the code for vulnerabilities. The key issue identified in the analysis is an off-by-one error in the grayscale bit processing.

Let's break down the vulnerability:

1. In the grayscale case (image->depth == 1), the code processes `number_bits` (capped at 8) bits from the raw data for each column `x`.
2. The inner loop increments `x` for each bit processed (so `x` becomes `x + number_bits`).
3. After the inner loop, the code checks if `x` is not equal to `image->columns` and then decrements `x` by 1 (with `continue` to skip the rest of the loop).

This decrement causes the next iteration to start at `x-1` (which is one less than the current `x`). 

Example with 10 columns:
- Start: x=0
- Process 8 bits (number_bits=8): x becomes 8 -> then decremented to 7.
- Next iteration: x=7 -> process 3 bits (number_bits=3): x becomes 10 -> no decrement (since 10 == 10).
- Total pixels processed: 8 (from x=0 to 8) + 3 (from x=7 to 10) = 11 pixels, but the image has only 10 columns.

This is an off-by-one error that causes one extra pixel to be processed.

The vulnerability is present because the code does not account for the fact that the inner loop already advanced `x` to the end of the image (or beyond) and the decrement is unnecessary and causes an extra pixel to be processed.

We must flag this as a vulnerability because it leads to incorrect pixel data (one extra pixel) and could cause other issues (like buffer overflows if the image buffer is not large enough).

Other potential issues (like endianness or bit order) are not as critical in this context because the code is designed for PSD files (which typically use big-endian for bit-packed data) and the author's explanation indicates the code is intended for that. However, the off-by-one error is a clear, concrete bug that affects correctness.

We'll output:

vulnerabilities: [ { "type": "Off-by-one error", "description": "The x variable is decremented after processing a bit stream when it hasn't reached the end of the image columns, causing one extra pixel to be processed." } ]
analysis: "The code decrements `x` after the inner loop for grayscale bit processing when `x` hasn't reached the image's column count. This causes the next iteration to start at `x-1`, resulting in one extra pixel being processed (e.g., 11 pixels for a 10-column image). This off-by-one error leads to incorrect pixel data."

rpmsg: virtio: Fix possible double free in rpmsg_virtio_add_ctrl_dev()

vch will be free in virtio_rpmsg_release_device() when
rpmsg_ctrldev_register_device() fails. There is no need to call
kfree() again.

```

commit_message:
Fix race condition in NewSessionTicket

If a NewSessionTicket is received by a multi-threaded client when
attempting to reuse a previous ticket then a race condition can occur
potentially leading to a double free of the ticket data.

CVE-2015-1791

This also fixes RT#3808 where a session ID is changed for a session already
in the client session cache. Since the session ID is the key to the cache
this breaks the cache access.

Parts of this patch were inspired by this Akamai change:
https://github.com/akamai/openssl/commit/c0bf69a791239ceec64509f9f19fcafb2461b0d3

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
(cherry picked from commit 27c76b9b8010b536687318739c6f631ce4194688)

Conflicts:
	ssl/ssl.h
	ssl/ssl_err.c
cve_desc: Race condition in the ssl3_get_new_session_ticket function in ssl/s3_clnt.c in OpenSSL before 0.9.8zg, 1.0.0 before 1.0.0s, 1.0.1 before 1.0.1n, and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2b, when used for a multi-threaded client, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (double free and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by providing a NewSessionTicket during an attempt to reuse a ticket that had been obtained earlier.

We are given a code snippet and the author's explanation. As a Security Analyst, I must identify vulnerabilities.

Key points from the code and explanation:

1. The function `ssl3_get_new_session_ticket` processes a session ticket message from the server.
2. It reads a 4-byte lifetime hint and a 2-byte ticket length (ticklen) from the message.
3. It checks if `ticklen + 6 == n` (where n is the total message length) to avoid length mismatches.
4. It then allocates memory for the ticket (of length `ticklen`), copies the ticket data, and computes a session ID by hashing the ticket data (using SHA256 or SHA1).

Potential vulnerability:

- The code does not check if `ticklen` is zero. If the server sends a ticket with `ticklen = 0`, then:
  - The session ID computation (`EVP_Digest(p, ticklen, ...`) will produce a session ID of length 0 (since the digest of 0 bytes is 0 bytes).
  - In TLS, session IDs must have a positive length (at least 1 byte). A zero-length session ID is invalid and would cause problems during session resumption (e.g., the server would not be able to match it).

This is a vulnerability because:
- The code does not validate that `ticklen` is positive.
- The absence of this check allows the creation of an invalid session ID (zero-length) which could lead to session resumption failures or other protocol issues.

Other considerations:
- The code checks `n >= 6` (to ensure at least 6 bytes for the header) but does not check that `ticklen` is positive.

commit_message:
Fix crash in MatrixSolve when inputs have different batch dimensions.

Before, the process would crash or certain elements would be silently ignored. Now an InvalidArgument is raised.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 384844020
Change-Id: Iba44417e383bdd0e1abc4012bfca83b2377dd335
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions several TensorFlow operations are missing validation for the shapes of the tensor arguments involved in the call. Depending on the API, this can result in undefined behavior and segfault or `CHECK`-fail related crashes but in some scenarios writes and reads from heap populated arrays are also possible. We have discovered these issues internally via tooling while working on improving/testing GPU op determinism. As such, we don't have reproducers and there will be multiple fixes for these issues. These fixes will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick these commits on TensorFlow 2.6.1, TensorFlow 2.5.2, and TensorFlow 2.4.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.
